dm: One should generate the mind without abiding in visible forms.
gm: they should produce the mind without dwelling on form.

dm: One should generate the mind without abiding in sounds, odors, tastes, tangible objects, or phenomena.
gm: they should produce the mind without dwelling on sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and dharmas.

dm: Subhūti, it is like this: for example, if a person were to have a body such as this, that is to say, if it were to become as large as Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, Subhūti, what do you think? Would that body be large?
gm: Subhūti, suppose, for example, a person were to have a body like this: that is, as large as Sumeru, the king of mountains. Subhūti, what do you think? Would you think that body is large?

dm: Subhūti replied, "Blessed One, that body would be large."
gm: Subhūti replied: Blessed One, that body would be large.

dm: "Sugata, that body would be large."
gm: Sugata, that body would be large.

dm: Why is that? Because the Tathāgata has taught that it is without any real entity.
gm: Why is that? Because the Tathāgata has taught it as being no entity;

dm: Therefore, it is called a large body.
gm: therefore, it is called a 'large body'.

dm: Because it is without any real entity, therefore it is called a body.
gm: Since it is no entity, therefore it is called a 'body'.

dm: The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, what do you think?
gm: The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think?

dm: If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, would the grains of sand in all those rivers be numerous?"
gm: If there were just as many Gaṅgā rivers as there are grains of sand in the Gaṅgā river, would you think that the grains of sand in them would be many?

dm: Subhūti replied, "Blessed One, those Ganges Rivers themselves would be numerous, so what need is there to mention the grains of sand in them?"
gm: Subhūti replied: Blessed One, if those Gaṅgā rivers themselves would be many, what need to speak of their grains of sand?

dm: The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, you must have faith.
gm: The Blessed One said: Subhūti, you should be convinced.

dm: You must understand this.
gm: You should understand.

dm: If a man or a woman were to fill as many world systems as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers with the seven types of precious jewels,
gm: If some man or woman were to completely fill as many world systems as there are grains of sand in those Gaṅgā rivers with the seven precious substances,

dm: and were to offer them as gifts to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly complete Buddhas, Subhūti, what do you think? Would that man or woman generate much merit on that basis?
gm: and give them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly and fully awakened Buddhas, Subhūti, what do you think? Would you think that man or woman would produce much merit from that basis?

dm: Subhūti replied, "Blessed One, it would be much."
gm: Subhūti replied: Blessed One, it would be much.

dm: "It would be much, Sugata."
gm: Sugata, it would be much.

dm: That man or woman would generate much merit on that basis.
gm: That man or woman would produce much merit from that basis.

dm: The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, if someone were to fill as many world systems as there are with the seven kinds of precious jewels and give them as a gift,
gm: The Blessed One said: Subhūti, if someone were to completely fill that many world systems with the seven precious substances,

dm: and were to offer them as gifts to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly complete Buddhas, compared to that, if someone were to take up even a four-line stanza from this Dharma discourse, and were to correctly explain and correctly teach it to others, that person would generate much more merit on that basis—countless and measureless merit."
gm: compared to giving them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly and fully awakened Buddhas, if someone were to take up even a four-line verse from this discourse on the Dharma, explain it fully and correctly to others, and teach it fully and correctly, they would produce infinitely and immeasurably much more merit from that basis.

dm: Furthermore, Subhūti, any place where even a four-line stanza from this Dharma discourse is recited or taught becomes a shrine for the world including gods, humans, and asuras. It goes without saying that anyone who takes up, writes down, holds, preserves, reads, masters, and properly attends to this Dharma discourse will be endowed with supreme wonder.
gm: Moreover, Subhūti, if the place where even a four-line verse from this discourse on the Dharma is recited or taught becomes a stūpa for the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, what need to speak of whoever takes up this discourse on the Dharma, writes it, holds it, keeps it, reads it, masters it, and attends to it properly becoming endowed with the greatest wonder?

dm: In that place, the Teacher or someone like a venerable guru resides.
gm: In that place dwells the Teacher, or someone like a guru.

dm: When he had spoken those words, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
gm: When this had been said, venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

dm: Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma discourse?
gm: Blessed One, what is the name of this discourse on the Dharma?

dm: How should it be remembered?
gm: How should it be held?

dm: When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti in this way:
gm: When this had been said, the Blessed One said this to venerable Subhūti:

dm: Subhūti, the name of this Dharma discourse is the Perfection of Wisdom;
gm: Subhūti, the name of this discourse on the Dharma is the Perfection of Wisdom, and

dm: hold it in this way.
gm: you should hold it thus.

dm: Why is that? Subhūti, because that which the Tathāgata has spoken of as the Perfection of Wisdom is itself not a perfection.
gm: Why is that? Subhūti, because the very perfection of wisdom that was taught by the Tathāgata is not a perfection.

dm: Therefore, it is called the Perfection of Wisdom.
gm: Therefore it is called the perfection of wisdom.

dm: Subhūti, what do you think?
gm: Subhūti, what do you think?

dm: Do you think that there is any Dharma whatsoever that has been spoken by the Tathāgata?
gm: Do you think there is any Dharma whatsoever that has been taught by the Tathāgata?

dm: Subhūti replied, “Blessed One, there is no Dharma whatsoever that has been spoken by the Tathāgata.”
gm: Subhūti said, "Bhagavān, there is no Dharma whatsoever that has been taught by the Tathāgata."

dm: The Blessed One said, “Subhūti, what do you think?
gm: The Bhagavān said, "Subhūti, what do you think?

dm: Do you think that the number of dust motes in the great trichiliocosm world system is many?”
gm: Do you think that the particles of earth that exist in the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system are many?"

dm: Subhūti replied, “Blessed One, those dust motes are many.”
gm: Subhūti said, "Bhagavān, those particles of earth are many.

dm: “They are many, Sugata.”
gm: Sugata, they are many.

dm: “Why is that? Blessed One, it is because the Tathāgata has taught that those dust motes are not dust motes.”
gm: Why is that? Bhagavān, because whatever is a particle of earth was taught by the Tathāgata as not a particle.

dm: Therefore, it is called "dust motes."
gm: Therefore it is called a particle of earth.

dm: Because the Tathāgata has taught that those world systems are not world systems.
gm: Because whatever those world systems are, they were taught by the Tathāgata as not systems.

dm: Therefore, they are called "world systems."
gm: Therefore it is called a world system.
